name: Engineering change to a released product (request to implementation)
summary: An engineering change alters a part, drawing, bill of materials or process for a product that is already in production, for example to fix a manufacturing problem, replace an obsolete component, cut cost or meet a customer request. A request is logged and triaged, a design engineer works out the change, manufacturing, purchasing, quality and planning each assess its impact, and a change control board approves it before the drawings, bill of materials and routings are updated, suppliers are told and the change is cut in at an agreed effectivity point. Each change touches six or more people, so most of its elapsed time is spent in engineering backlogs, waiting for reviewers, the weekly board, signatures, supplier quotes and the next production run. Errors come from incomplete requests, missed affected items, hand re-keying between the PDM and the ERP, and old-revision stock being used after the change.

baseline.org_archetype: A discrete manufacturer of engineered industrial equipment with about 800 employees, one main plant, ISO 9001 certification, a PDM system with a change workflow that is not linked to the ERP, and some customers in regulated supply chains who require change notification.
baseline.notes: One case is one change request of any size. About a third are minor document or drawing changes on a fast track; the rest go through full impact analysis and the board.

unit_of_work: one engineering change request and the resulting change order
trigger: A change request is submitted for a part, drawing, bill of materials or process of a released product.
end_state: The change is released, the bill of materials, routing and documents are updated, the change is cut in at its effectivity point with first units inspected and the record is closed; or the request is rejected.

volume.seasonality: Fairly steady; peaks after new product launches and when a component goes obsolete.

evidence.note: src1 reports MAPI member companies handling about 34 minor and 24 medium ECOs a month; MAPI members are mostly large, so the mode for an 800-person manufacturer is set below that total.

triggered_by.from: Engineering cost reduction and product improvement

produces.object: released drawings, bill of materials, routing and work instructions
new drawing revision and revised purchase orders
change record with review and authorization

roles.title: Change requester (engineer, quality, service or sales staff)

evidence.note: Blended cost of the people who raise change requests; most are engineers or technicians. Based on the engineer and technician wages in src10 loaded at 1.7.

Change analysts vet changes and run the CCB agenda (src2). Nearest SOC is Industrial Engineering Technologists and Technicians, median $28.95. Loaded cost = BLS May 2021 median hourly wage x 1.7 (1.50 benefits from BLS ECEC December 2021 for manufacturing, about 1.13 overhead by author estimate).

Triages requests, chairs the change board and signs changes. Median $73.25. Loaded cost = BLS May 2021 median hourly wage x 1.7 (1.50 benefits from BLS ECEC December 2021 for manufacturing, about 1.13 overhead by author estimate).

Mechanical Engineers median $45.82. About 25 design engineers in the archetype spend roughly a quarter of their time on changes to released products, within the one-third to one-half range reported in src1. Loaded cost = BLS May 2021 median hourly wage x 1.7 (1.50 benefits from BLS ECEC December 2021 for manufacturing, about 1.13 overhead by author estimate).

Assesses routing, tooling and work instruction impact. Industrial Engineers median $45.82. Loaded cost = BLS May 2021 median hourly wage x 1.7 (1.50 benefits from BLS ECEC December 2021 for manufacturing, about 1.13 overhead by author estimate).

Assesses quality impact, runs first article inspection. Nearest SOC is Industrial Engineers, median $45.82. Loaded cost = BLS May 2021 median hourly wage x 1.7 (1.50 benefits from BLS ECEC December 2021 for manufacturing, about 1.13 overhead by author estimate).

Gets supplier quotes and notifies suppliers. Buyers and Purchasing Agents median $30.51. Loaded cost = BLS May 2021 median hourly wage x 1.7 (1.50 benefits from BLS ECEC December 2021 for manufacturing, about 1.13 overhead by author estimate).

Checks stock and open orders and sets effectivity and disposition. Production, Planning and Expediting Clerks median $23.10. Loaded cost = BLS May 2021 median hourly wage x 1.7 (1.50 benefits from BLS ECEC December 2021 for manufacturing, about 1.13 overhead by author estimate).

systems.name: Product data management (PDM) or basic PLM with change workflow
ERP (item master, bills of materials, routings, purchasing, inventory)
Quality records system or controlled document library

steps.name: Raise engineering change request
steps.description: Someone who has found a problem or an opportunity, such as a manufacturing engineer, quality engineer, service technician or salesperson relaying a customer request, fills in the change request form in the PDM workflow or on a paper or spreadsheet form, describing the part, the problem, the proposed change and its urgency.
inputs: problem report, customer request or idea

error.defect_description: Request lacks part numbers, reason or evidence, or proposes a solution without describing the problem.

evidence.note: A change starts with a request on a standard form giving reason, priority and type (src6). Time is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Log request and check completeness
steps.description: The change analyst opens the new request, checks that part numbers, revision, reason and supporting evidence are present, gives it a number in the change log and returns it to the requester if information is missing.

error.defect_description: Request logged against the wrong part revision.

next.condition: returned to the requester for missing information

evidence.note: Change analysts vet changes before review (src2); the form goes to a change controller who enters it in a database (src6). The 15% return rate is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Triage, classify and assign
steps.description: At the weekly triage review the engineering manager reads the request, decides whether it is worth doing, classifies it as minor or major by its effect on form, fit, function, cost and customers, sets a priority and assigns a design engineer.

error.defect_description: Change classified as minor when it affects fit or a customer-controlled characteristic.

control.basis: Company engineering change procedure (ISO 9001:2015 clause 8.5.6): changes are reviewed before work starts

next.condition: not worth doing or a duplicate

evidence.note: Classification by effect on form, fit, function and cost (Class 1 and 2) is described in src7; approval authority set by significance in src9. The weekly triage rhythm and 8% rejection rate are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Develop the design solution
steps.description: The design engineer reviews the problem, works out a solution, usually just one, and changes the CAD model, drawing or specification, checking tolerances and the parts it mates with. Small changes take an hour or two; a redesigned part can take several days of work.

error.defect_description: Solution misses an interface with a mating part or a variant of the product.

evidence.note: Solutions are developed after the request, and often only one is considered (src6). The wait reflects the engineering backlog; src1 reports ECO work takes one-third to one-half of engineering capacity. Hours are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Look up where-used, stock and open orders
steps.description: The design engineer runs a where-used report in the PDM and ERP to list every assembly and product that uses the part, and pulls stock on hand, work in progress and open purchase orders so the impact reviewers can see what is affected.

error.defect_description: An affected assembly is missed because the ERP and PDM structures differ.

next.condition: minor change: drawing note, document or non-fit change, fast track
change affects parts, process, suppliers or stock: full impact analysis

evidence.note: The ECO lists all affected parts and assemblies (src3); impact analysis determines affected components (src6). The 50% fast-track share follows the MAPI mix of 34 minor to 24 medium ECOs a month reported in src1 (59% minor), reduced because some minor changes still touch stock or suppliers.

steps.name: Prepare minor change package
steps.description: For a minor change the design engineer marks up the drawing or document, fills in the short change order with reason and affected items, sets the disposition of existing stock to use as is and submits it for electronic approval.

error.defect_description: Revision letter or affected item list wrong.

evidence.note: Minor ECOs take about 4 days on average (src1); ECO content from src3. Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Approve minor change
steps.description: The engineering manager, and in many companies a quality engineer as second signer, opens the change order in the PDM workflow, checks the markup and the classification and signs it or sends it back with a comment.

error.defect_description: Approval given without opening the drawing.

control.basis: ISO 9001:2015 clause 8.3.6 (retain records of design changes, review results and who authorised them), required by the company's certified quality system

evidence.note: ISO 9001 8.3.6 requires records of the authorization of changes (src8); slow approvers are a main cause of delay (src2). The 10% return rate is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Release minor change and update records
steps.description: The change analyst releases the new drawing or document revision in the PDM, withdraws the old revision from the shop document folders, updates the item revision in the ERP and notifies the affected departments by email.

error.defect_description: Old revision left in a shop folder or ERP revision not updated.

control.basis: ISO 9001:2015 clause 7.5.3 control of documented information (version control, only current revisions at the point of use)

evidence.note: Version control of documented information (src8); ensuring only current documentation reaches manufacturing is a known problem (src6). Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Assess manufacturing impact
steps.description: The manufacturing engineer reviews the proposed change against the routing, fixtures, tooling, machine programs and work instructions, estimates the cost and time to change them, and notes whether the change can be made on the current line.

error.defect_description: Tooling or fixture change overlooked, found at cut-in.

evidence.note: Impact assessment across design, suppliers and budget is a phase of the change process (src6, src9). Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Assess purchasing impact and ask for quotes
steps.description: The buyer checks which purchased parts are affected, looks at open purchase orders and supplier stock, and emails the supplier the proposed drawing to ask for price, lead time and any tooling charge for the new revision.

error.defect_description: Quote requested on the wrong drawing revision.

evidence.note: Supply chain partners take part in change review (src3) and supplier effects are part of impact assessment (src6). Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait for supplier quote and lead time
steps.description: The supplier reviews the drawing and replies with price, lead time, tooling cost and sometimes a capability concern. Buyers often follow up by phone when the reply is slow.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

evidence.note: Supplier quote turnaround of one to eight days beyond the time already spent in the other concurrent reviews is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Assess quality and customer impact
steps.description: The quality engineer reviews the change against the inspection plan, risk analysis and control plan, decides whether first article inspection or testing is needed, and checks customer agreements to see whether the customer must be notified or must approve.

error.defect_description: Customer notification requirement missed.

control.basis: ISO 9001:2015 clause 8.5.6: changes are reviewed to the extent needed to ensure continuing conformity

evidence.note: Review of changes for continuing conformity and records of the review (src8, src9). Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Assess stock and propose effectivity
steps.description: The materials planner checks stock, work in progress and open orders of the old revision, works out the cost of scrapping, reworking or using it up, and proposes an effectivity date or serial number and a disposition code for each item.

error.defect_description: Stock at a subcontractor or in transit missed, so old parts are built after the change.

evidence.note: ECOs carry manufacturing disposition codes (src3); obsolete stock is a common surprise at review (src6). Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Compile impact assessment
steps.description: The change analyst collects the manufacturing, purchasing, quality and stock notes into the change record, totals the one-time and unit cost effects and checks which reviewers have not yet responded.

error.defect_description: Cost effect totalled from an outdated quote.

evidence.note: Collecting impact across functions before board review (src2, src6). The 30% overdue share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Chase overdue impact reviews
steps.description: The change analyst emails and phones the reviewers who have not responded, escalating to their managers when the change is urgent, and records the replies when they arrive.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

evidence.note: Unavailable reviewers and unclear ownership stall changes (src2). Wait and effort are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Finalise drawings and BOM redline
steps.description: The design engineer updates the model and drawings to reflect review comments, prepares the bill of materials redline showing added, removed and changed lines, and attaches the final documents to the change order.

error.defect_description: BOM redline quantity or find number wrong.

evidence.note: The ECO includes drawings, revision details and affected parts (src3). Hours are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Build change order package and schedule board review
steps.description: The change analyst assembles the change order: reason, affected items, redlines, impact assessment, cost, effectivity and disposition proposal, checks it for completeness and adds it to the next change board agenda.

error.defect_description: Package goes to the board missing a document, causing a repeat review.

evidence.note: Changes are routed to the CCB with a documented package; poor documentation causes repeat cycles (src2). Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Change board review
steps.description: At the weekly change control board, chaired by the engineering manager with members from design, manufacturing, quality, purchasing, planning and service, the engineer presents the change and the board approves it, sends it back for more work or rejects it. The time shown is total attendee time for this one change.

error.defect_description: Board approves a change whose effectivity conflicts with a customer commitment.

control.basis: Configuration control board approval under the company change procedure, giving the review and authorization records ISO 9001:2015 clauses 8.3.6 and 8.5.6 require

next.condition: sent back for more analysis or corrections

evidence.note: Board membership and approve, return or reject outcomes (src6, src7); repeated CCB entries add elapsed time (src2). Branch probabilities and per-change time are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Send change notice to customer
steps.description: The quality engineer prepares the customer change notice with the reason, the old and new drawings, the validation plan and proposed effectivity, and submits it through the customer's portal or by email as the quality agreement requires.

error.defect_description: Notice omits a characteristic the customer controls.

control.basis: Customer contract or quality agreement requiring notice and approval of changes to form, fit, function or process (for example PPAP resubmission in automotive supply)

evidence.note: Customer notification for significant changes is common in automotive, aerospace and medical supply chains; effort is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait for customer approval
steps.description: The customer's engineering or quality team reviews the notice and may ask for samples or test data before approving. The change cannot be released until approval arrives.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

evidence.note: Customer approval turnaround of one to six weeks is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Collect change order signatures
steps.description: The change order is routed in the PDM workflow to the required signers, typically the design engineer's manager, manufacturing engineering, quality and purchasing, each of whom opens it and signs or rejects it. The time shown is the total for all signers.

error.defect_description: Signer approves without checking the redline.

control.basis: Company change procedure: the author of a change cannot approve it; independent signatures give the authorization record required by ISO 9001:2015 clause 8.3.6

next.condition: a signer rejects for an error in the package

evidence.note: Approval routing with required approvers versus observers and slow approvers (src2); authorization records (src8). Rates are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Release change and update BOM in ERP
steps.description: The change analyst releases the new revisions in the PDM, then keys the bill of materials changes, new item numbers and revision levels into the ERP by hand because the two systems are not linked, and withdraws superseded drawings from the shop.

error.defect_description: BOM line keyed with wrong quantity or effectivity, found when the line builds.

control.basis: ISO 9001:2015 clause 7.5.3 control of documented information (only current revisions at the point of use)

evidence.note: Version control (src8); updating paperwork and keeping only current documents in manufacturing (src6). Re-keying between PDM and ERP is the author's estimate of common practice without integration.

steps.name: Update routing and work instructions
steps.description: The manufacturing engineer changes the routing operations and standard times in the ERP, edits the work instructions and inspection sheets, and asks for machine program or fixture changes where needed.

error.defect_description: Work instruction still shows the old part.

evidence.note: Implementation includes updating documents and informing affected staff (src9, src6). Hours are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Notify suppliers and revise purchase orders
steps.description: The buyer sends the new drawing revision to the supplier, changes or cancels open purchase orders for the old revision, places orders for the new one and asks the supplier to confirm the delivery date.

error.defect_description: Supplier keeps shipping the old revision against an unchanged order line.

next.condition: new purchased parts needed before cut-in
no new purchased parts, or stock of the new part already available

evidence.note: Supply chain partners are part of ECO approval and execution (src3). The 40% share needing new parts is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait for new-revision parts
steps.description: The supplier makes or modifies tooling and ships the first lot of the new revision. Receiving checks the revision on arrival.

error.defect_description: Supplier ships parts to the old drawing.

evidence.note: Remaining lead time for a modified purchased part of three to thirty days is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Set effectivity and disposition stock
steps.description: The materials planner enters the effectivity date or serial number in the ERP, flags old-revision stock as use as is, rework, return to supplier or scrap according to the approved disposition, and adjusts planned orders so the switch happens on time.

error.defect_description: Effectivity date set before new parts arrive, causing a shortage.

control.basis: Company change procedure: disposition of superseded stock as approved in the change order; nonconforming stock handled under ISO 9001:2015 clause 8.7

evidence.note: Disposition codes are part of the ECO (src3); nonconforming outputs are controlled under 8.7 (src8). Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Cut in the change on the line
steps.description: When the effectivity point arrives, the production supervisor briefs the operators, makes sure old-revision parts are segregated, checks the new work instructions are at the station and runs the first units with the change.
outputs: first units built to the new revision

error.defect_description: Old-revision part used by mistake.

evidence.note: Waiting for the next production run of the product and the time to brief and build are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Inspect first units
steps.description: The quality engineer measures the first units or parts against the new drawing using gauges and fixtures, records the results on a first article report and either accepts the cut-in or raises a problem that sends the change back to manufacturing engineering.
inputs: first units built to the new revision

error.defect_description: Characteristic not measured.

control.basis: Company procedure and customer requirements for first article inspection after a design change (AS9102 in aerospace supply chains)

next.condition: problem found with routing, instructions or parts

evidence.note: Verification after implementation and review of whether the change achieved its aim (src9, src6). Rates and hours are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Close the change order
steps.description: The change analyst checks that every action on the change order is done, attaches the first article report and supplier acknowledgements, closes the record in the PDM and change log and files it as a quality record.

error.defect_description: Record closed with an open action.

control.basis: ISO 9001:2015 clauses 8.3.6 and 8.5.6: retain documented information on the change, its review, authorization and resulting actions

evidence.note: Records of the change and its actions (src8); the closing review is often skipped or late (src6). Wait is the author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Incomplete request returned
exceptions.description: The change analyst returns the request for missing part numbers, reason or evidence.

exceptions.name: Request rejected at triage or by the board
exceptions.description: The change is judged not worth doing, a duplicate, or too risky.

exceptions.name: Overdue impact reviews chased
exceptions.description: One or more reviewers have not responded and the analyst chases them, adding days.

exceptions.name: Board sends change back
exceptions.description: The board asks for more analysis or corrections, so the package goes round again and waits for the next meeting.

exceptions.name: Customer approval required
exceptions.description: A form, fit, function or process change needs the customer's written approval before release.

exceptions.name: Signer rejects the package
exceptions.description: A signer finds an error in the redline or documents after the board has approved it.

exceptions.name: Waiting for new-revision parts
exceptions.description: Cut-in waits until the supplier delivers parts to the new drawing.

exceptions.name: First article problem
exceptions.description: First units show a routing, instruction or part problem that manufacturing engineering must fix before acceptance.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days to process an ECO
benchmarks.population: MAPI member manufacturers, as reported by src1: medium ECOs average 17 days; minor ECOs 4 days; major ECOs 109 to 142 days

evidence.note: p50 is the reported average for medium changes and p90 the lower estimate for major changes. These figures measure ECO processing; this workflow also includes the cut-in and first article after release, so a simulated median above 17 days is expected.

benchmarks.population: More than 4,000 organisations in APQC benchmarking, as quoted by src5

evidence.note: Secondary report of an APQC measure; the start and end points of the APQC measure are not stated.
Vendor case study; shows how far a manual multi-database process can stretch.
Major changes per month not reported.

benchmarks.population: One automotive firm (Boznak 1993) cited in src6

evidence.note: Administrative processing only; about $41 million a year in total at that firm.

benchmarks.unit: share of new product development cost (median)
benchmarks.population: 325 organisations in APQC benchmarking, as quoted by src5

evidence.note: Secondary report of an APQC measure.

benchmarks.population: Practitioner targets from a PLM vendor

evidence.note: Targets from the author's experience, not measured averages.

pain_points.description: Changes wait in the engineering backlog because the same engineers also work on new products; the ECO process is said to take one-third to one-half of engineering capacity.

evidence.note: Claim reported without a named source in src1.

pain_points.description: Impact reviewers and signers respond late or not at all, and changes stall without escalation.

evidence.note: Slow and unavailable approvers and unclear ownership (src2).

pain_points.description: Poorly documented changes re-enter the board, each time waiting for the next weekly meeting.

evidence.note: Repeated CCB entries add elapsed time (src2).

pain_points.description: The bill of materials is re-keyed from the PDM into the ERP, and errors surface only when the line builds.

evidence.note: Common in companies whose PDM and ERP were not integrated in 2019 to 2022; author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Old-revision stock or documents are used after the change because effectivity and segregation are not tight.

evidence.note: Ensuring only current documentation reaches manufacturing is a frequent problem (src6).

sources.title: 7 Symptoms of an Engineering Change Order Bottleneck
sources.supports: Reports a MAPI member survey: minor ECOs take 4 days on average (34 a month), medium ECOs 17 days (24 a month), major ECOs 109 to 142 days; says many organisations report the ECO process takes one-third to one-half of engineering capacity and that 73% do not know the cost of ECOs (both without a named source).

sources.title: What's Killing Your Change Review Cycle Times?
sources.supports: Change review flow from creation through manager and change analyst vetting to CCB entry and approval; common targets of five days for ECOs and ten days for ECRs; causes of delay such as repeated CCB entries, poor documentation, slow or unavailable approvers and too many approvers.

sources.title: Engineering Change Order (ECO) Definition
sources.supports: ECO lists affected parts and assemblies, reason, drawings, manufacturing disposition codes, revision and cost information; ECOs are reviewed and approved by internal teams and supply chain partners through a change control board.

sources.title: How a top manufacturer reduced cycle times by 84% with PLM
sources.supports: Case of Teradyne: change order cycle times cut from 90 days to 14 days after centralising engineering change management in PLM.

sources.title: Engineering KPIs That Actually Predict Delivery (and the Ones That Do Not)
sources.supports: States that APQC cross-industry benchmarking puts the median ECO cycle time at 7.0 days across more than 4,000 companies and ECO cost at a median 10.0% of new product development cost across 325 companies (secondary report of APQC data).

sources.title: The Impact of Engineering Change Request (ECR) on Accuracy of Project CEAC (master's thesis, J. Razi)
sources.supports: Literature review: an automotive firm (Boznak 1993) spent $41 million a year on administrative processing of change requests, about $1,400 per request; about 95% of UK design-and-make firms had a formal engineering change procedure (Huang and Mak 1999); Jarratt's six-phase change process (request, solutions, impact assessment, change board approval, implementation, review) with iterations back to earlier phases.

sources.title: Engineering Change Proposal (ECP)
sources.supports: Configuration management practice: Class 1 and Class 2 change classification, change impact analysis and risk assessment, configuration control board decision, no implementation until the change is authorised.

sources.title: "Documented Information" in ISO 9001:2015 (handout with clause excerpts)
sources.supports: ISO 9001:2015 text: 7.5.3 control of changes (version control); 8.3.6 retain documented information on design changes, results of reviews, authorization of changes and actions to prevent adverse impacts; 8.5.6 retain the results of review of changes, the persons authorizing and necessary actions; 8.7 nonconforming outputs.

sources.title: Clause 8.5.6 ISO 9001 2015 Explained
sources.supports: Common implementation of change control: documented procedure covering initiation, review, approval, implementation and verification; impact assessment; approval authority by significance; communication and training of affected staff; records of request, rationale, approval and actions.

sources.title: May 2021 National Occupational Employment and Wage Estimates, United States
sources.supports: Median hourly wages: Mechanical Engineers 17-2141 $45.82; Industrial Engineers 17-2112 $45.82; Architectural and Engineering Managers 11-9041 $73.25; Industrial Engineering Technologists and Technicians 17-3026 $28.95; Buyers and Purchasing Agents 13-1020 $30.51; Production, Planning and Expediting Clerks 43-5061 $23.10; First-Line Supervisors of Production and Operating Workers 51-1011 $29.71.

sources.title: Employer Costs for Employee Compensation - December 2021 (news release)
sources.supports: Manufacturing: total compensation $41.13 per hour, wages and salaries $27.38 (66.6%), benefits $13.76 (33.4%).

assumptions: One case is one change request of any size. Branch probabilities give about 46% minor fast-track changes, 43% full changes and 11% rejected, roughly following the minor to medium mix in src1.

The cycle_time_days benchmark measures ECO processing. The simulated overall median (about 17 days) falls between the two main paths: minor fast-track changes have a simulated median of about 13 days and full changes about 44 days. Minor changes run slower than the 4-day MAPI figure because this workflow starts at the request and includes triage and the engineering backlog; full changes run longer than the 17-day medium figure because this workflow continues past release through supplier parts, cut-in and first article inspection.
Impact reviews by manufacturing, purchasing, quality and planning run at the same time in practice; they are listed in sequence with short waits and named in concurrent_with.
Board and signature steps record total attendee or signer minutes under the engineering manager's role, so their labour cost is priced at the manager's rate.
The FTE stated for design engineers includes only time on changes to released products, not new product work.
Loaded hourly cost is the BLS May 2021 national median wage for the nearest SOC code times 1.7 (1.50 benefits from BLS ECEC December 2021 for manufacturing, about 1.13 overhead by author estimate).
Most hours, waits and rework rates are tier C estimates; sources give processing times and process descriptions but rarely hands-on effort.
